subject: model comparison loglikelihood vs fit indices

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: model comparison loglikelihood vs fit indices
parts:
Hi mirt community

I have an intersting/weird results for a model comparison. 

I am comparing 2 models: 1 factor, vs 7 factors, graded response models. Due to the large number of factors I am using MHRM as the estimation method.

When doing the model comparison it shows that the 7 factor model is better, this makes sense so far
> anova(mirt_1f, mirt_6f)

Model 1: mirt(data = dat2, model = 1, itemtype = "graded", SE = T, method = "MHRM", 
    technical = list(NCYCLES = 2000))
Model 2: mirt(data = dat2, model = m6f, itemtype = "graded", SE = T, method = "MHRM", 
    technical = list(NCYCLES = 2000))

        AIC     AICc    SABIC       HQ      BIC    logLik      X2  df   p
1 10011.289 9052.154 9916.658 10297.69 10716.52 -4752.644     NaN NaN NaN
2  9785.097 8812.839 9682.612 10095.27 10548.87 -4618.549 268.191  21   0


But when I look at the fit indices of each model the 1 factor model has a better fit based on RMSEA, and CFI
> round(mfit_1f,4)### 1 factor
                M2   df p  RMSEA RMSEA_5 RMSEA_95  SRMSR    TLI    CFI
stats    2124.8859 1125 0 0.0864  0.0804   0.0916 0.1002 0.9152 0.9190
SD_stats   26.6904    0 0 0.0012  0.0012   0.0011 0.0007 0.0021 0.0021
> round(mfit_6f,4)### 7 factor
                M2   df p  RMSEA RMSEA_5 RMSEA_95  SRMSR    TLI    CFI
stats    4798.7643 1104 0 0.1677  0.1622   0.1719 0.3589 0.6779 0.6979
SD_stats   34.6265    0 0 0.0008  0.0008   0.0008 0.0025 0.0043 0.0040


How come the loglikelihood comparison shows better fit for the 7 factor, but the fit measures are better for the 1 factor? Which one is a better way to select the best structure?

Any help would be greatly appreciated

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: model comparison loglikelihood vs fit indices
parts:
The likelihood ratio test is likely more accurate here, particularly if you didn't use the QMC option in M2. The former test when using the MH-RM algorithm computes the log-likelihood via stochastic integration, so should be relatively free of the "curse-of-dimensionality" problem, whereas M2 computes the values using standard numerical integration (which gets less accurate as the number of traits increases). That would be my first guess.

Phil

Given the "curse of dimensionality", the M2 fit indices are not as reliable then? 

I ask because I am used to evaluate fit from the SEM perspective, and coming from that having a better likelihood but worst RMSEA doesnt make sense. Clearly I dont know the difference of those in IRT.

A side question about MHRM, is this bayesian estimation or is it using the metropolis hastings for integration in the maximum likelihood? As this is the type of sampler that Stan uses for general bayesian. 

Thank you for the great program

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: model comparison loglikelihood vs fit indices
parts:
On Tue, Jun 26, 2018 at 3:59 PM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:
Phil

I did use QMC=T for M2. So, for model selection I would trust more the likelihoods. 

Given the "curse of dimensionality", the M2 fit indices are not as reliable then?

I think at some point and for some models the M2 statistic could break. Like all statistics it's possible for it to fail for numerical reasons as well, so it's possible there's just something extreme about your observations causing problems too (e.g., intercepts could be too large, slopes are tending to infinity, etc). It's likely too hard to tell without looking rather close to a reproducible example.

I ask because I am used to evaluate fit from the SEM perspective, and coming from that having a better likelihood but worst RMSEA doesnt make sense. Clearly I dont know the difference of those in IRT.

RMSEA is a function of the degrees of freedom and general goodness of fit as a chi-square variate, so more complicated models often can and do have larger RMSEA values if the decrease in df and model fit are not traded off well (that's largely the point of these fit stats, and is true in SEM as well). This is also true of the other measures CFI, TLI, etc. The log-likelihood test just states that one model is more likely than the other in terms of predicting the data, not that it is an effective representation of the data or that the (potentially large) decrease in df (and therefore increase in model complexity). 

That all said, the log-likelihood and M2 statistics really are focusing on different data aspects. M2 is focusing on uni/bivariate moments only, and collapsing the high-dimensional tables of counts to these moments, while the log-likelihood is computed row-wise in the data itself and therefore contains all moments without collapsing.

A side question about MHRM, is this bayesian estimation or is it using the metropolis hastings for integration in the maximum likelihood? As this is the type of sampler that Stan uses for general bayesian.
Just as an integration for the random effect components. It only becomes a Bayesian estimator if you include prior parameter distributions explicitly. HTH.

Thank you for the great program
